papers.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.brief: A deep convnet, trained on GPUs, beat the field at image classification and made representation learning the default bet.
papers.question: What would break if you applied ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
papers.brief: Adaptive per-parameter step sizes from first and second moments. Know what the bias correction is doing, and when AdamW is the version you actually want.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Adam without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
papers.brief: Residual connections let very deep nets train. The idea travels: a skip is how you keep a signal alive through a stack of layers.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Attention Is All You Need
papers.brief: Self-attention replaces recurrence. Queries, keys, and values are the whole mechanism, and the cost is quadratic in sequence length.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Attention Is All You Need without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers
papers.brief: Masked language modeling makes a transformer useful as a representation, not only as a left-to-right generator.
papers.question: What would break if you applied BERT without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
papers.brief: Scale plus next-token training produces in-context learning. The paper is as much about what you no longer fine-tune as about the model.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Language Models are Few-Shot Learners without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
papers.brief: Loss falls as a power law in parameters, data, and compute. The allocation between them is the decision.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
papers.brief: For a fixed compute budget, earlier models were under-trained. Tokens should scale with parameters.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
papers.brief: Supervised demonstrations, then a reward model, then RL. Alignment here is a product pipeline, not a single loss.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.brief: Freeze the base weights and train a low-rank update. Adaptation becomes cheap enough to keep one base and many tasks.
papers.question: What would break if you applied LoRA without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention
papers.brief: Exact attention, tiled so the score matrix never lands fully in slow memory. IO is the bottleneck, not the FLOPs on paper.
papers.question: What would break if you applied FlashAttention without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Direct Preference Optimization
papers.brief: Preference pairs can train the policy directly. The reward model and the RL loop are not the only way to use comparisons.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Direct Preference Optimization without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events
papers.brief: Happened-before is a partial order. Logical clocks exist because wall clocks cannot be trusted to agree.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree
papers.brief: Absorb writes in memory, flush sorted runs, merge them later. Write amplification is the bill you pay for that shape.
papers.question: What would break if you applied The Log-Structured Merge-Tree without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: The Google File System
papers.brief: Large files, append-heavy workloads, and a single master with the metadata. Failures are normal, not exceptional.
papers.question: What would break if you applied The Google File System without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
papers.brief: A tiny programming model on top of a hard distributed system: placement, shuffle, stragglers, and re-execution.
papers.question: What would break if you applied MapReduce without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data
papers.brief: A sparse sorted map on tablets. Locality comes from the key order you choose, not from the storage layer guessing.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Bigtable without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
papers.brief: Consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, and hinted handoff. Availability wins, and conflicts become the application's problem.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Dynamo without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Paxos Made Simple
papers.brief: A quorum agrees on one value even when messages are lost and proposers compete. Read it until the two phases feel inevitable.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Paxos Made Simple without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: The Chubby Lock Service
papers.brief: A coarse lock and naming service that people used as a source of truth. Reliability and a small API beat a clever one.
papers.question: What would break if you applied The Chubby Lock Service without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: ZooKeeper: Wait-free Coordination
papers.brief: A totally ordered wait-free API for coordination recipes: locks, membership, and configuration, built on a consensus core.
papers.question: What would break if you applied ZooKeeper without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm
papers.brief: Leader election, log replication, and safety told as one story. Understandability is a design requirement.
papers.question: What would break if you applied In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
papers.brief: External consistency across datacenters, with TrueTime bounding clock uncertainty so timestamps can order transactions.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Spanner without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing
papers.brief: A partitioned, replayable log. Consumers pull, retention is the buffer, and the log outlives any one subscription.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Kafka without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
papers.brief: Information, entropy, and the idea that a channel has a capacity. Compression and noise are the same subject.
papers.question: What would break if you applied A Mathematical Theory of Communication without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Learning representations by back-propagating errors
papers.brief: Credit assignment through a stack of layers by the chain rule. Everything later is an implementation of this.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Learning representations by back-propagating errors without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition
papers.brief: A full pipeline: pixels, convolution, subsampling, and a trained classifier, on a real document problem.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Long Short-Term Memory
papers.brief: Gates keep a memory cell from vanishing or exploding across long gaps. The cell is the product, the recurrence is the carrier.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Long Short-Term Memory without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting
papers.brief: Randomly drop units in training so the network cannot rely on a single co-adapted path.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Dropout without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Batch Normalization
papers.brief: Normalize inside the network so each layer sees a steadier distribution. It changes the optimization landscape, not just the scale.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Batch Normalization without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes
papers.brief: An encoder, a decoder, and a latent distribution you can sample. The ELBO is the compromise you can actually optimize.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Generative Adversarial Nets
papers.brief: A generator and a discriminator in a game. The training target is a moving one, which is why it is powerful and brittle.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Generative Adversarial Nets without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization
papers.brief: Nets can memorize noise and still generalize on real data. Classical capacity stories are not enough.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
papers.brief: A dense net contains sparse subnetworks that, trained from their original initialization, match the dense net.
papers.question: What would break if you applied The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Deep Double Descent
papers.brief: The bias-variance U-shape returns, then test error falls again as models become heavily overparameterized.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Deep Double Descent without the assumption the authors relied on?

papers.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
papers.brief: Learn to reverse a noise process, one small step at a time. Sampling quality comes from many cheap denoising steps.
papers.question: What would break if you applied Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models without the assumption the authors relied on?

posts.title: One stream, two performances
posts.dek: A face and a voice that stay in time are an inference problem, not a chatbot with a portrait.
posts.author: Study desk
body: A talking face that matches a voice is easy to demo and hard to serve. The interesting constraint is not the avatar. It is that one generated stream has to drive two performances, sound and motion, and both have to arrive before the silence feels broken.

Causal generation matters here. The model cannot wait for a full utterance, render a video, and then start playback. Each chunk has to be produced from what has already been said, and the next chunk has to continue from that state. That is the same prefill-and-decode tension as a text model, with a frame budget instead of a token budget.

Once you look at it that way, the product questions get concrete. How many sessions fit on a GPU if each one holds its own state? What is the acceptable motion lag before the face and the voice split? Which part of the pipeline is memory-bound, and which part is waiting on the network?
This note is an original study essay. It is not a reprint of any article on the reference site.

posts.title: The agent forgets, even when the model doesn't
posts.dek: Most of what a modern agent learns lives outside the weights.
posts.author: Study desk
body: A frozen model does not forget a fact it was trained on. An agent still can. Prompts, memory files, tool lists, and routing rules are part of the behavior, and they change on a different schedule from the weights.

That split is useful. You can fix a tool schema without a training run. It is also how last week's reliable path quietly dies: a skill file was edited, a memory note was compacted, a router started sending a class of questions somewhere else.

Treat those artifacts as code. Version them, review them, and keep a small eval set that fails when a change costs you a behavior you meant to keep. A gate that only commits a change when the old cases still pass is a product decision, not a research slogan.
This note is an original study essay about the idea, written for this build.

posts.title: Most of an AI request is waiting
posts.dek: A chat endpoint spends almost none of its life computing.
posts.author: Study desk
body: Draw a four-second request as a bar. The model call is a slice. DNS, TLS, queueing, retrieval, tool round-trips, and the client's patience are the rest. If you only optimize the slice you can see in a profiler, you will miss the wait.

Waiting is why async earns its keep in an AI backend, and why a bigger worker pool does not help a service that is blocked on one remote call. The concurrency lab on this site is the same picture with a slider.

Once the bar is honest, architecture choices get quieter. Cache the retrieval. Stream the tokens so the user is not staring at the full wait. Put a timeout on every outbound call, including the model.

posts.title: Three flavors of simulating an agent pipeline
posts.dek: An eval that only checks a frozen answer will miss a pipeline that fails in motion.
posts.author: Study desk
body: The cheapest simulation replays a transcript. You pin the model outputs and check that your tool router and your state machine do what they did last time. It is a regression test. It will not tell you whether a new prompt still reaches the right tool.

The next flavor stubs the model with a small scripted policy: given this state, emit this tool call. You can walk the pipeline through branches without paying for tokens and without pretending the script is a language model.

The expensive flavor calls the real model on a small set of tasks and scores the trace: did it stop, did it ask for approval, did the side effect happen once. Run that set when the prompt, the tools, or the model version change. Use the cheaper two on every commit.

news.title: Frontier models keep showing up as product surfaces
news.dek: A new model release matters here when it changes latency, context, or the tool-use loop, not when it changes a leaderboard screenshot.

news.title: Voice interfaces are still waiting on turn-taking
news.dek: Speech products fail in the pause between sentences. The serving budget is the conversation, not the word error rate alone.

news.title: On-device and hosted models are a routing choice
news.dek: Local models win on privacy and tail latency for short prompts. Hosted models win when the quality gap is still the product.

news.title: Data-center power is now part of the design doc
news.dek: A serving plan that ignores energy, water, and community constraints is an incomplete capacity plan.

news.title: Agent products are growing a permission layer
news.dek: The interesting ship this season is not another planner. It is the sandbox, the approval step, and the trace you can read after a bad run.

news.title: Eval sets are leaving the notebook
news.dek: Teams that can describe a regression in a trace will outrun teams that only have a vibe check channel.

news.title: Chip diversity is a portability problem
news.dek: A stack that runs on one vendor's kernel library will meet a second vendor the week capacity gets tight.

news.title: Long context does not remove retrieval
news.dek: A bigger window changes the cutoff. It does not make unscoped search free, and it does not make stale documents fresh.

faqs: Start free. If you want to build AI backends in Python, open Python with AI. If you want to know how models are actually served, open Inference Engineering. If you want architecture judgment and interview practice, open System Design.
What is actually inside Inference Engineering?
How models are served: GPUs and memory, the KV cache, batching, quantization, speculative decoding, parallelism and autoscaling, with the arithmetic worked in the open.
What is actually inside Python with AI?
Python through FastAPI, Pydantic, streaming, agents, MCP and tracing. One support-agent project is carried through the path.
What is actually inside System Design?
Notes, case files, and from-scratch implementations: requests, storage, caches, queues, search, realtime, and the interview shapes those ideas show up in.
Is this only for interview prep?
System Design is useful in an interview because it is useful on the job. The other two tracks are about building and serving, not about a whiteboard ritual.
It is not part of this copy. Each lesson still has its own video, the notes, and a check you answer yourself.
How often does the material change?
Lessons are revised when the underlying tools change. This study build snapshots the path structure and writes original notes, so it will not track upstream edits automatically.
